# 2 Samuel Chapter 14 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 183v–184v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_014_page_001.jpg, 2SA_014_page_002.jpg, 2SA_014_page_003.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king's heart longed for Absalom.

**2** So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought from there a wise woman. He said to her, "Pretend to be a mourner and put on mourning garments. Do not anoint yourself with oil, but be as a woman who has been mourning many days for the dead.

**3** Then go to the king and speak to him in this manner." And Joab put the words in her mouth.

**4** When the woman of Tekoa came to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and bowed down and said, "Save me, O king!"

**5** The king said to her, "What is your trouble?" She said, "Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead.

**6** Your servant had two sons. They quarreled with one another in the field, and there was no one to separate them, and the one struck the other and killed him.

**7** Now the whole clan has risen against your servant, and they say, 'Give up the one who struck his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed, and destroy the heir as well.' They would quench my last remaining ember, leaving to my husband neither name nor remnant on the face of the earth."

**8** The king said to the woman, "Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you."

**9** The woman of Tekoa said to the king, "On me be the guilt, my lord the king, and on my father's house; let the king and his throne be guiltless."

**10** The king said, "If anyone speaks against you, bring him to me, and he shall not touch you again."

**11** Then she said, "Please let the king invoke the LORD your God, that the avenger of blood not destroy further, lest they destroy my son." He said, "As the LORD lives, not a hair of your son shall fall to the ground."

**12** Then the woman said, "Please let your servant speak a word to my lord the king." He said, "Speak."

**13** The woman said, "Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in giving this verdict the king convicts himself, inasmuch as the king does not bring back his own banished one.

**14** We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not simply take away life; rather, he devises plans so that the banished one may not remain an outcast from him.

**15** Now I have come to speak this word to my lord the king because the people made me afraid. Your servant thought, 'I will speak to the king; perhaps the king will grant the request of his servant.

**16** For the king will hear, and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would cut off both me and my son from the inheritance of God.'

**17** And your servant thought, 'The word of my lord the king will set me at rest,' for my lord the king is like the angel of God in discerning good and evil. May the LORD your God be with you."

**18** Then the king answered the woman, "Do not hide from me anything I ask you." The woman said, "Let my lord the king speak."

**19** The king said, "Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?" The woman answered, "As surely as you live, my lord the king, one cannot turn to the right or to the left from anything my lord the king has said. It was your servant Joab who commanded me; he put all these words in the mouth of your servant.

**20** In order to change the course of the matter, your servant Joab did this. But my lord has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God, to know all things that are on the earth."

**21** Then the king said to Joab, "Behold, I grant this. Go, bring back the young man Absalom."

**22** Joab fell on his face to the ground and bowed down and blessed the king. And Joab said, "Today your servant knows that I have found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, in that the king has granted the request of his servant."

**23** So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.

**24** But the king said, "Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face." So Absalom returned to his own house and did not see the king's face.

**25** Now in all Israel there was no man so praised for his beauty as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

**26** And when he cut the hair of his head — at the end of every year he used to cut it, for it was heavy on him — he weighed the hair of his head: two hundred shekels by the king's weight.

**27** There were born to Absalom three sons and one daughter whose name was Tamar. She was a woman beautiful in appearance.

**28** So Absalom lived in Jerusalem two full years without seeing the king's face.

**29** Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but Joab would not come to him. He sent a second time, but he would not come.

**30** Then he said to his servants, "See, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire." So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.

**31** Then Joab arose and went to Absalom at his house and said to him, "Why have your servants set my field on fire?"

**32** Absalom answered Joab, "Look, I sent word to you, saying, 'Come here, that I may send you to the king to ask, "Why have I come from Geshur? It would have been better for me to remain there."' Now let me see the king's face, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death."

**33** So Joab went to the king and told him. And he summoned Absalom, and he came to the king and bowed with his face to the ground before the king. And the king kissed Absalom.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators agree on the narrative structure: Joab's scheme (vv.1-3), the wise woman's parable (vv.4-11), the theological pivot (vv.12-17), David's detection and concession (vv.18-24), Absalom's description and partial exile (vv.25-28), and the burning field resolution (vv.29-33). The wise woman's speech in v.14 is recognized by all three as the theological center of the chapter. The Masoretic text is stable throughout, with no major variant requiring adjudication.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "perceived" vs. "knew" vs. "could see"
- **EMET:** "And-knew Yo'av"
- **LOGOS:** "Joab perceived"
- **PNEUMA:** "Joab could see"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Joab perceived." The Hebrew *vayeda'* means "knew/perceived." LOGOS's "perceived" captures both the cognitive and intuitive dimensions of Joab's discernment.

### V.1 — "heart was set on" vs. "heart was upon" vs. "heart longed for"
- **EMET:** "the-heart of-the-king [was] upon Avshalom"
- **LOGOS:** "the king's heart was set on Absalom"
- **PNEUMA:** "the king's heart longed for Absalom"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the king's heart longed for Absalom." The preposition *'al* is ambiguous, but context from 13:39 indicates yearning. PNEUMA's "longed for" makes the emotional content explicit and is consistent with the preceding verse.

### V.4 — "Save me" vs. "Help me"
- **EMET:** "Save [hoshi'ah], O-the-king!"
- **LOGOS:** "Save me, O king!"
- **PNEUMA:** "Help me, your majesty!"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Save me, O king!" The Hebrew *hoshi'ah* specifically means "save/deliver" — a stronger appeal than PNEUMA's "help me." LOGOS preserves the urgency and the specific verb.

### V.7 — "my last remaining ember" vs. "my coal"
- **EMET:** "my-coal [gachalti]"
- **LOGOS:** "my last remaining ember"
- **PNEUMA:** "my last glowing ember"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "my last remaining ember." LOGOS's expansion makes the metaphor clear in English without over-interpreting. PNEUMA's "glowing" adds a detail not in the text, though evocative.

### V.13 — "devised" vs. "done"
- **EMET:** "have-you-devised [chashavta]"
- **LOGOS:** "have you devised"
- **PNEUMA:** "have you done"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "have you devised." The Hebrew *chashav* means "to think/plan/devise" — not merely "to do." The verb carries intentionality. LOGOS/EMET are correct.

### V.14 — "God does not take away life" vs. "God doesn't just snatch life away"
- **EMET:** "And-not does-God take-away a-life [nefesh]"
- **LOGOS:** "God does not take away life"
- **PNEUMA:** "God doesn't just snatch life away"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "God does not simply take away life." Combining LOGOS's formality with PNEUMA's qualifying "simply/just," which captures the nuance — God *could* take life but chooses restoration instead.

### V.20 — "to turn around the face of the matter" vs. "to change the course of affairs" vs. "to approach the matter from a different angle"
- **EMET:** "In-order to-turn-around [the]-face of-the-matter"
- **LOGOS:** "In order to change the course of affairs"
- **PNEUMA:** "to approach the matter from a different angle"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "In order to change the course of the matter." A blend: LOGOS's structure with EMET's "the matter" (singular, as in the Hebrew *davar*).

### V.25 — "beautiful" vs. "praised for his beauty" vs. "admired for his appearance"
- **EMET:** "a-man beautiful [yafeh]"
- **LOGOS:** "no man so praised for his beauty"
- **PNEUMA:** "no one was more admired for his appearance"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "no man so praised for his beauty." LOGOS captures both the Hebrew *lehallel* (to praise) and *yafeh* (beautiful) in a single dignified phrase.

### V.26 — "two hundred shekels" weight conversion
- **EMET/LOGOS:** Retain "two hundred shekels by the king's weight" (EMET notes ~2.3 kg)
- **PNEUMA:** "five pounds by the royal standard"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "two hundred shekels by the king's weight." The ancient measurement should be preserved in the text; conversions belong in footnotes. PNEUMA's conversion is approximate and removes the textual specificity.

### V.32 — "Good for me while I was still there" vs. "It would have been better for me to remain there"
- **EMET:** "Good for-me [while]-I [was]-still there"
- **LOGOS:** "It would have been better for me to remain there"
- **PNEUMA:** "I'd be better off still there"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "It would have been better for me to remain there." LOGOS captures the force of Absalom's bitter complaint in dignified English. PNEUMA is too colloquial for royal speech to the king.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
